note.text: Premises are the offered reasons; a conclusion is the claim they support. The inference is the move from reasons to that claim, not another quoted person or a punctuation mark. Background may explain the setting without functioning as a reason. A conclusion can come first, last or in the middle. Reconstruct complete claims and preserve their qualifications. Calling something a premise does not establish that it is true.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to extract complete premises and conclusion while separating background and inference. Builds on: arguments and intended support. Leads to: indicators and later analysis of a whole passage.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original passage: At a club meeting, Bih argues that the notice needs correction. The room is still provisional, but the notice calls it confirmed. Therefore its venue statement misrepresents the arrangement. The meeting location is background; the mismatch is the reason; the notice judgement is the conclusion.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Underline the target claim, bracket each offered reason and mark contextual material separately. Rewrite each relevant claim as a full sentence without changing its scope. Ask how the premises are meant to support the target.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve scope, terms and assumptions.
example: Every premise is guaranteed true because it is named a premise. Correction: A role in an argument does not establish factual truth.
A conclusion must be the passage’s final words. Correction: Its role, not position, identifies it.
The word therefore alone is the complete conclusion. Correction: The conclusion is a claim; therefore signals the move.
Every detail in a passage must be a premise. Correction: Some details provide context rather than support.
